In brief

Parody. "Love loves to love love […] everybody loves somebody but God loves everybody": after Bloom says that the point of life is love rather than hatred, and the Citizen laughs at the notion of a Jew preaching the Christian gospel of "Universal love," and John Wyse Nolan sympathetically recalls Jesus's famous admonition—"Isn't that what we're told. Love your neighbour"—this short paragraph mocks the notion that Love makes the world go 'round. Its sarcastically childish voice implies that the cultivation of love in Christian societies is simpleminded treacle.

At more length

Bloom has not alluded to any religious or metaphysical doctrines, but the Citizen assumes he is talking about something of the kind: "— A new apostle to the gentiles, says the citizen. Universal love." The word could also refer to romantic sexual love, however, and for good measure he knocks Bloom on that score too: "He's a nice pattern of a Romeo and Juliet." The parody ridicules both kinds of love. It starts with a bit of metaphysical-sounding nambypamby mumbojumbo ("Love loves to love love"), then runs though a highly mundane list of romantic lovers, and concludes with a bromide that mimics actual Christian teaching ("everybody loves somebody but God loves everybody").

Gifford discerns a plausible model for the first statement in Augustine's Confessions, "describing his immersion in sexual desire before he discovered that God was the true and ultimate object of love and desire": "Not yet did I love, though I loved to love, seeking what I might love, loving to love" (3.1). The second statement derives ultimately from the gospel of John: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life" (John 3:16). The writer of three epistles traditionally attributed to the apostle John elaborated on this theme: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.... Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another. No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us.... God is love. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God in him" (1 John 4:8-10, 12, 16).

Certain writers of the later Middle Ages—Bernard of Clairvaux, Hildegard of Bingen, Julian of Norwich—worked to replace the old picture of God as an angry judge with the view that God is more like a compassionate mother or an ardent bridegroom. Even Dante, unsurpassed in justifying the cosmic order imposed by an angry judge, himself approached God through the love of Beatrice and defined the deity as "the Love that moves the sun and all the other stars" (Paradiso 33.145). Joyce's beloved Thomas Aquinas embraced John's saying that "God is love" and reasoned that this love must be both universal and more unselfishly generative than human love: "God loves all existing things. For all existing things, in so far as they exist, are good.... it is manifest that God loves everything that exists. Yet not as we love.... our will is not the cause of the goodness of things, but is moved by it as by its object...whereas the love of God infuses and creates goodness in things" (Summa Theologica 1.20.2).

All of these writers assume, not an equivalence, but a linkage between two kinds of "love": the sexual hunger that impels people to mate and raise families, and the spiritual longing that unites creatures with their Creator. Joyce's parody effects the same linkage. Between its two metaphysical gestures comes a flippant, tawdry, vaguely comical list of people who love other people, all of them quasi-anonymous, not-quite-real, cardboardy figures. The effect of reading the list is totally unlike watching Romeo and Juliet, and a lot like hearing about "lovely Rita, meter maid," or learning that "Her Majesty's a pretty nice girl, but she doesn't have a lot to say."

Many of the people are as close to anonymous as can be. The "Nurse" and her "chemist," and "M.B." and her (or his) "fair gentleman," do not even receive names. "Constable 14A," also unnamed, was mentioned earlier in Cyclops, unnamed there too, and the "Mary Kelly" he loves, Gifford notes, "is so common that it suggests 'any Irish girl'." "His Majesty the King" may love "Her Majesty the Queen," but they exist only as titles, not as Edward and Alexandra. "Li Chi Han" and "Cha Pu Chow" may contain certain buried Chinese meanings, as both Gifford and Slote suppose, but their effect seems mainly to insinuate some sniggling racist laughter. "Mrs Norman W. Tupper" comes from a photograph seen earlier in Cyclops, sitting in the lap of her "officer Taylor" rather than that of her husband, a wealthy Chicago contractor. "Old Mr Verschoyle with the ear trumpet" and his wife, "old Mrs Verschoyle with the turnedin eye," may refer to some actual Dubliners—both Gifford and Slote offer possibilities—but if so, who cares?

Only three items linger in memory for more than an instant. "Gerty MacDowell" and "the boy that has the bicycle" will be identified in the following chapter. "The man in the brown macintosh" was seen in Hades and again in Wandering Rocks, and learning that he "loves a lady who is dead" adds a tantalizingly concrete detail to the mystery of who he might be. Most touching of all the love stories is the news that "Jumbo, the elephant, loves Alice, the elephant." These were actual elephants at the Royal Zoological Gardens in London. When P. T. Barnum bought Jumbo in 1882 and shipped him over to America to display as the world's largest, Alice was reportedly distraught. In My Brother's Keeper Stanislaus Joyce recalls Mrs. Riordan, when her husband abandoned her and fled to South America, writing to him Alice's lines in a popular song: "if you really loved me, / As you say you do, / You'd never go to Yankee Town / And leave me in the zoo" (9).

Clearly this string of silly, inconsequential amours, credulously trotted out in the lisping tones of a nursery rhyme, is intended to ridicule the notion that our trivial human couplings somehow illustrate the beneficent divine order of the universe. And so, like all the other parodies, this one uses a gigantic exaggeration (God loves everybody) to mock mundane reality. But in other ways this interruption is atypical. It does not take aim at the trendy preoccupations of the Irish Literary Revival or the patriotic bluster of the Citizen and his supporters, as most of the parodies do. Instead, like the account of "distinguished scientist Herr Professor Luitpold Blumenduft" (mocking Bloom's pretension of knowing some science) and the "Klook klook klook" account of a hen (mocking his concern for animal welfare), it takes on Joyce's protagonist, poor Leopold. And it does so just as he voices what seems to be a cherished authorial conviction in this jocoserious novel: that love, whether romantic or familial or more broadly social, is the best creed available to human beings. 

Many people who find Christian eschatology intolerable or distasteful nevertheless find much to value in Christian ethics, and James Joyce was arguably one of those people. His hero is not a believer, but he is charitable in the Christian sense of imaginatively empathizing with others and doing what he can to help them. When Bloom says, "That's not life for men and women, insult and hatred [...] everybody knows that it's the very opposite of that that is really life," he is referring not just to the romantic love binding couples but to the impulse to make the world a less vicious place. An Aquinian sentence that Joyce wrote for Scylla and Charybdis shows that he did not separate the sexual affection he found to be imperative in his own life from the social benevolence preached by the church he had left. Stephen is searching for sexual happiness but thinks of the Augustinian distinction between desiring things for one's own good (cupiditas) and loving them for another's good (caritas). Leopold Bloom embodies both sexual and charitable love—and in the twelfth chapter he is mocked for both.

John Hunt 2026
